title: Accidents, Near Misses & RIDDOR
whatItIs: RIDDOR 2013 is the law that makes employers and people in control of work premises report and record certain work-related accidents, diseases and dangerous occurrences (near misses).

keyFacts.text: Deaths and specified injuries MUST be notified without delay, with a report received within 10 days.
An injury that keeps a worker off normal work for over 7 days in a row MUST be reported within 15 days.
Injuries causing over 3 days off normal work MUST be recorded, but needn't be reported.
A member of the public hurt and taken from the scene to hospital for treatment MUST be reported.

keyFacts: The 7 days don't count the day of the accident, but do count weekends and rest days.

visual.caption: What RIDDOR says must be reported, and when

a.label: Specified injury
points: Eg a fracture (not finger, thumb or toe), amputation, loss of consciousness
Notify without delay; report within 10 days

b.label: Over-7-day injury
points: Off work or unable to do normal duties for over 7 days in a row
Report within 15 days of the accident

onTheTest.question: A worker breaks his arm in a fall from a trestle. When must this be reported under RIDDOR?
options: Without delay, with a report received within 10 days
Only if he's off work for over 7 days
Only if he stays in hospital overnight
onTheTest.why: A fracture other than to a finger, thumb or toe is a specified injury. The enforcing authority must be notified without delay and a report received within 10 days.

onTheTest.question: A labourer strains her back at work and can't do her normal job for 5 days. What does RIDDOR require?
options: Record it, but it doesn't need reporting
onTheTest.why: Over-3-day injuries must be recorded (the accident book is enough). They only have to be reported if the incapacity goes on to exceed 7 days.

traps: Count weekends: the 7 days exclude the day of the accident but include rest days.
A broken finger, thumb or toe isn't a specified injury, but it may still be an over-7-day injury.
Near misses count: some dangerous occurrences must be reported even if no one is hurt.
